reason: This passage from 2 Kings 22-23 describes King Josiah's religious reforms and his leadership role, but does not assert that the elite are inherently better than regular people. While the text depicts social hierarchy (with the king at the apex directing priests and officials), righteousness and righteousness are measured by obedience to God's Law, which applies universally to all people. Notably, the text explicitly includes all classes in the covenant-making ceremony ('from the least to the greatest'), and actually critiques the corrupt religious practices of the elite priests and previous kings. The narrative evaluates people's worth based on their adherence to divine commandment, not their social status.
